newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says Belarus strife internal, urges calm.
newsitem.headline: Russia says Belarus strife internal, urges calm.

text.p: Russia called on the authorities and opposition in Belarus on Monday to show more tolerance and negotiate an end to their confrontation, but said a recent crackdown on protests was an internal matter.
"The events in Belarus are an internal affair of that country," President Boris Yeltsin's chief spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told Interfax news agency.
He said he did not expect arrests of anti-government protesters to affect Moscow's plans for closer integration with its western neighbour.
Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko is due to meet Yeltsin for new talks on integration in Moscow on April 2 -- the first anniversary of a treaty setting up a two-nation "community".
Both presidents say they are working towards an eventual "union" of the two former Soviet states, and the Kremlin indicated it saw its role as a conciliator inside Belarus.
"Everyone knows the role played by Russia, which has frequently called for reconciliation between the two opposing sides in Belarus," Yastrzhembsky said.

"The message with which Russia addressed both sides, calling on them to show more patience and to seek and find solutions to their problems not through confrontation but with the aid of national accord and dialogue, is once more relevant," he added.

Last November, Russia brokered a compromise between the 42-year-old Lukashenko and his opponents in parliament, who were attempting to block the president's move to take substantial new powers through a referendum.

In an embarrassment for Moscow, however, Lukashenko then pushed through the referendum anyway, winning a clear mandate that allowed him to scrap the old parliament and set up a new one more to his liking.
The president has cracked down on protests this month in the capital, Minsk, organised mainly by nationalist groups opposed to his plans to reunite with Russia.
The United States has cut off aid to Belarus and on Monday issued a strong protest at Minsk's decision to expel a U.S. diplomat arrested at a protest rally on Sunday.

Russian television journalists, whose broadcasts are widely received in Belarus, said they were barred from Minsk's main television centre on Monday, preventing them transmitting reports. Lukashenko strictly controls the Belarussian media.
Other foreign television journalists said they too were denied access to the broadcasting centre.
The Glasnost Fund media rights group in Moscow called on the Russian government to defend Russian journalists' rights in Belarus.
Some analysts see Yeltsin's recently renewed interest in union with Belarus as partly a response to planned expansion into eastern Europe by NATO, the Western defence pact.

Closer ties with Belarus also help deflect some criticism inside Russia, where the communist- and nationalist-dominated parliament accuses Yeltsin of breaking up the Soviet Union and has made rebuilding Moscow's old empire one of its goals.
